concept.name: Suitability
concept.definition: The FINRA Rule 2111 obligation that a broker-dealer or associated person have a reasonable basis to believe that a recommended transaction or investment strategy is suitable for the customer, based on reasonable diligence to ascertain the customer's investment profile — including age, other investments, financial situation and needs, tax status, objectives, experience, time horizon, liquidity needs, and risk tolerance. For retail customers, suitability has been superseded by Regulation Best Interest (SEA Rule 15l-1), to which Rule 2111 no longer applies.
concept.intuition: A broker can't sell you just anything that isn't fraudulent — the recommendation has to fit who you are, what you can afford, and what you're trying to do.
concept.mechanics: The rule has three components: reasonable-basis suitability (the product must be suitable for at least some investors, based on understood risks and rewards), customer-specific suitability (it must fit this customer's profile), and quantitative suitability (a series of trades must not be excessive taken together). Institutional accounts may qualify for an exemption if they can evaluate risks independently and affirmatively exercise independent judgment.
concept.failure_modes: Suitability is judged at the recommendation point, so a 'suitable' product can still be a poor investment; profiles built on customer self-reporting can be gamed (e.g., inflated risk tolerance to permit risky sales), and the standard historically allowed conflicted recommendations that met the floor but served the broker's compensation.
concept.misconceptions: Suitability never meant 'best available' or guaranteed performance — it was a minimum-fit standard, which is precisely why Reg BI replaced it for retail recommendations; and it applied only to recommendations, not to unsolicited trades a customer directs.
concept.example: Recommending a leveraged inverse ETF as a long-term hold to a 70-year-old widow with a conservative profile and short liquidity horizon would violate customer-specific suitability even if the ETF is a legitimate product.

citations.source: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), via Internet Archive snapshot of finra.org
